title: Will a film made in Bremerton answer a secret about Bigfoot?
excerpt: A child in South Kitsap suspected a secret. It kicked off a search for answers in 'Capturing Bigfoot,' a film made in Kitsap coming to Amazon Prime.
content:
Oct. 12, 2026, 4:01 a.m. PT

"Teresa, don't worry about it. I'm Bigfoot."

With those words, Norm Johnson tucked his daughter, then around 9 years old, into bed in their South Kitsap home. It was the early 1970s in the Pacific Northwest, and little Teresa Johnson could sense the cultural milieu. A grainy film clip, caught on 16-millimeter tape and purportedly showing the legendary Bigfoot in Northern California, was making headlines and appearing on the TV news and even movie theaters, and naturally was talked about at South Colby Elementary. The little girl likely wasn't the only one wondering if a furry cryptid could be wandering around her neighborhood.

But the young Teresa, now Teresa Brooks, was satisfied by her father's bedtime assurance, and slept soundly, she said in a September interview in Bremerton. It rarely came up again.

Fifty years later, she may finally understand what he meant. And along with a Bremerton filmmaker, is going to share a story with a wider community that may, or may not, contain an answer.

Interest big enough for Amazon

Marq Evans is a documentary filmmaker, last profiled in the Kitsap Sun when his independently financed film, "The Diamond King," debuted in 2025. That documentary made the rounds of some film festivals and baseball card conventions (the subject was a painter bridging the arts and sports worlds), screened locally for a modest crowd at the Roxy Theatre, can be bound on PBS or streaming, and earned some applause at a Seattle Mariners game, where one of the film's actors threw out the first pitch before a game that summer.

This October Evans finds himself in a much different public relations atmosphere, with his latest work scheduled to launch on Amazon Prime's national platform, a podcast series already launching backstory episodes for an audience of paid subscribers, a social media blitz featuring Evans himself in front of the camera, and screenings coming up in San Francisco, Seattle, New York, Los Angeles, Dallas, Bremerton and, notably to this story, Yakima.

The film is "Capturing Bigfoot," which at one point Evans thought would be a cowboy movie centered on a cast of characters in the region of Central Washington where he grew up. It turned into a project that encompassed five years, consisted of piles of documents and hours of archived audio, witnessed wrenching personal interviews and even tapped into Evans' own past as he tracked down reclusive participants to examine an unknown side of a story that has captivated conspiracy theorists and Sasquatch enthusiasts for five decades.

"It's a great story, with great characters... that happens to be on the subject of Bigfoot," Evans said.

And it just happened to fall in his lap, or more specifically his laptop's email, serendipitously because Evans now lives in Kitsap County.

A nearly forgotten film, and a story that could have been lost

Norm Johnson died in 2009, after raising his family in Kitsap and a career that included an early stint at Boeing and then running J&J's Print Shop on Callow Avenue, with his wife Sharon. He had been a coin collector, and his daughter Teresa Brooks remembered being the one sibling allowed to watch dad stack his new finds in a family safe. She remembered a reel of film that was always tucked into that safe, though never discussed. Even her mother, after Norm Johnson's passing in 2009, didn't want to talk about it, but when Sharon Johnson died in 2017, the film was a heirloom Brooks knew was worth keeping. Without equipment to play the keepsake, she risked mailing it away to a Costco photo development site, but it came back along with a converted DVD showing what had been recorded.

What she saw had everything to do with the nightmares of her childhood, and her dad's calming words.

Brooks found the footage fascinating, but her children did not, she said, and there wasn't interest in looking more closely into what grandpa may have been doing back then. But an old friend of Norm's in South Kitsap, Ray Bricker, was interested in talking about the old days. Bricker eventually emailed Brooks in the fall of 2021, she said, encouraging her to share the film. Maybe call Debbie Macomber, the nationally known Port Orchard author, he suggested. She could write a book.

Except this was a film. And Brooks, who now works at Olympic College teaching social sciences, knew the Bremerton campus had a relatively new film program. So she emailed the department head the next summer, asking, "Do you want to figure out what this film is?"

And Marq Evans, who was eventually on the end of her forwarded email, did.

A 'mystery that kicked the whole thing off'

Evans sent the original 16-millimeter film footage to a North Carolina company, which scanned it into a higher resolution digital file. The film showed a scene, which was believed to be from rural Yakima County, that strongly resembled the footage known as the Patterson-Gimlin film. That's the widely seen, flickering movie of a brown, furry biped more than seven feet tall, walking in a canyon near the Klamath River in 1967. In the film the creature, dubbed "Patty," appears to pause slightly and look back at the camera, which came into American consciousness in the late '60s and remained a subject for years, whether it proved the sasquatch exists or was a hoax to debunk. You've likely seen the clip, or seen its cultural ripple in silhouette images of Bigfoot walking and offering what may be a slight wave, from bumper stickers to road signs to all sort of sasquatch ephemera.

The Patterson-Gimlin film was made by Bob Gimlin and Roger Patterson, the latter a self-made icon from Yakima that Evans is now illustrating through a podcast and social media posts, also named "Capturing Bigfoot." Patterson spent the 1960s exploring the wilderness of Central Washington searching for Bigfoot, documenting much of it, even writing books about his belief in the legend.

The Patterson-Gimlin film had been dated to fall 1967, the year it was also shown in several cities across the United States and caught part of the nation's attention. It could be dated based on a coding material that identified Kodachrome film of that era, Evans said. Using the same clues in looking at Norm Johnson's film, he determined that one was made in 1966... and was remarkably similar to the one that made waves and spawned all sorts of interest.

"What does that mean?" Evans remembered thinking at the time, recounted during a recent interview. "Are they connected? And they are definitely connected."

A book, a connection, and a family opens up

Evans began reading up on Patterson and the film, including the 2004 book "The Making of Bigfoot," by Greg Long. Evans contacted Long, who was forthcoming in sharing his research into Roger Patterson and Bob Gimlin, including 100 hours of recorded interviews he had done. Evans listened to them, and found what was more than just a tenuous connection between the famous film and the story of a Port Orchard family was learning. One interview Long had done, which wasn't included in the book, connected directly to Norm Johnson, through his brother, Dave, who had lived in Yakima.

Evans called upon his own family ties at that point, asking a relative who worked in the trades around Yakima if he knew any connections to Patterson's family. That question led him to interviews with longtime Yakima residents who'd been around Patterson or the group filming in the 1960s, and Gimlin himself, as well as family members who'd never talked about their father's fame. Eventually they'd talk, some of whom admitted revisiting the famous film would cause rifts, but also help address some long buried feelings.

"He told us, 'I've been waiting to tell this story and get things off my chest," Evans said of one of the key interviews for the documentary, Patterson's son Clint. "He'd always wanted to do that, and this was the perfect opportunity."

The film leans into those interview in trailers, many of them done in Montana, where some of the Pattersons, including Robert's widow Patty, live now. But it remains strongly connected to Yakima, Evans' hometown, where "Capturing Bigfoot" will screen on Oct. 24.

"(Capturing Bigfoot) is about these people, and what that film had done to people's lives. There's a curse on (the Patterson-Gimlin) film, a lot of lives have been ruined," Evans said. "It's about reconciliation too, and bringing stuff back together."

National interest, but still a family's story

"Capturing Bigfoot" debuted in March at the South by Southwest film festival, in Austin, Texas. But Evans and his team declined other festival invitations, preferring to keep the footage away from the many sasquatch skeptics and supporters until this fall's larger launch.

Brooks' family, however, was able to gather and see whether Norm Johnson was involved in a dress rehearsal of the Bigfoot walk through California. Part of his involvement was due to his brother, but also explained by his job at Boeing, where he was in the film department in the 1960s. He had skills with editing tape and access to equipment. So Evans arranged for a day when more than 50 of Johnson's relatives, some in the area and others who flew in from places like California, could meet for a private screening at the log cabin next to Peninsula Bible Fellowship in Central Kitsap.

"My whole family just stood and clapped, they were crying," Brooks said of the family's showing.

The night was similar to all showings so far in that Evans and the management team has carefully guarded the footage that was buried in Johnson's safe. Patrons have not been allowed to bring phones or wear glasses with capability to record, to bar any illicit recording of the new footage. And no leaks have surfaced in the Reddit threads among Bigfoot enthusiasts who, Evans says, are abuzz with anticipation for what the new evidence means to the legend.

"People are saying that 'Capturing Bigfoot' is the biggest things to happen to Bigfoot since the Patterson film," Evans said.

That's why this story can't tell readers how it ends, or what exactly the footage, which found its way serendipitously to West Bremerton, may or may not prove. Like the Sasquatch, the truth remains elusive. As does Teresa Brooks' understanding of her father, in some ways.

"My dad was a fun guy, I can see him being part of this," Brooks said during an interview in Bremerton, noting she think Johnson would be happy with how the film turned out.

But still, she said the story, at least for her, hasn't been unraveled completely.

"I don't know why he kept it such a secret," Brooks said, but then speculated, putting herself in her dad's mind. "Maybe, let Teresa (share it) when I'm gone."

"Capturing Bigfoot," distributed by XYZ Films, premieres on Amazon Prime on Oct. 20. It will play in Bremerton on Oct. 30, in a special screening at the Roxy Theatre where Evans and Brooks will appear, including an interview and Q&A after the film.
